title: A good apology
hookLine: a study by Roy Lewicki and colleagues found the most important parts are owning responsibility and offering repair

cards: "I'm sorry if anyone was offended." It has the word sorry right there in it, and still it can land like a door clicking shut.
So can its cousins: sorry you feel that way, mistakes were made, I said I was sorry, what more do you want? Each one is an apology that somehow isn't one.
A team of researchers led by Roy Lewicki took apologies apart, piece by piece, to find out which pieces actually do the work.

teach.b: Lewicki and his colleagues listed the parts an apology can have: saying you regret it, explaining what went wrong, acknowledging that you're responsible, saying you've changed, offering to repair the damage, and asking to be forgiven.
Then they asked people to judge apologies built from different mixes of those parts.
The piece that mattered most was acknowledging responsibility. Next came offering repair. And the piece that mattered least was asking for forgiveness.
The apology works best when it's about what the speaker did and will do, and least when it asks something of the person who was hurt. Look at the door-clicking apology again.

teach.h: IF ANYONE WAS OFFENDED OWNS NOTHING.
teach.b: "If anyone was offended" doesn't own anything. Its subject is the other person's feelings, not the speaker's action. Owning sounds like a sentence with I at the front: I did this, and it was wrong.
Repair answers the next question: and here's what I'll do about it. An older text sets the same order, and makes it urgent.

In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus describes someone bringing a gift to the altar who remembers there that a brother has something against him: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."
The repair comes before the worship. The text doesn't wait for the brother to come asking; the one at the altar gets up and goes. And the gift waits there until he's back.

how: Researchers who study apologies, including Roy Lewicki and colleagues, describe an effective apology as one that clearly acknowledges responsibility and offers to repair the harm; in Matthew 5, reconciliation comes before offering a gift at the altar.

it mattered least. acknowledging responsibility mattered most, then offering repair.

games.q: you snapped at a coworker in a meeting. which apology has the two parts the study found mattered most?
o: "I was wrong to snap at you. I'll set it right with the team today."
games.why: it owns it, starting with I, and it offers repair. the other two either own nothing or lean on the part that mattered least: asking for forgiveness.

practice: Choose one person you owe an apology to, small or large, and build it in your head from just two parts: own it, starting with I, I did this and it was wrong; then repair, here's what I'll do.
Notice any urge to add a but, an if, or an explanation, leave it off, and say the two sentences once more, slowly, as if they were listening.
